The quoted passage establishes that aleatoric probability requires frequentist estimation from large ensembles, not axiomatic derivation. This leads to a duality: while aleatoric uncertainty can be modeled mathematically via relative frequencies, its empirical estimation suffers from finite-sample bias and non-ergodic breakdowns. In GSI, this manifests as overfitting risk bounds under distributional shift. In GSE, it corresponds to unreliable stochastic dynamics when training data does not span the operational state space.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The frequentist definition traces back to von Mises' collectives (1919) and Kolmogorov's measure-theoretic foundations (1933). Ramsey (1926) introduced the separation between objective chance and subjective belief, while Knight (1921) formalized the distinction between risk and uncertainty. Savage (1954) later incorporated both into expected utility theory.
